titleEn: Laws of Hammurabi — Epilogue III: the curses of Ea, Šamaš, Sîn and Adad (xlii 98 – xliii 80)
part: Epilogue III · the curses of Ea, Šamaš, Sîn and Adad (Col. xlii 98 – xliii 80)
about: The third part of the epilogue goes on with the curses on a later king who destroys or alters the stele, each god taking a turn. Ea, the great prince who knows everything and lengthens the king’s days, is asked to turn wisdom and understanding away from the wrongdoer, to bring him to oblivion, to dam up his rivers at the source, and to keep Ašnan, the grain, the life of the people, from growing in his land (xlii 98 – xliii 13). Šamaš, great judge of heaven and earth, is asked to overthrow his kingship, to refuse him justice, to confuse his road, to destroy the foundation of his army, to set before him an evil omen, to let the grievous word of Šamaš overtake him quickly, to uproot him from among the living and to deprive his spirits of water in the earth (xliii 14–40). Sîn, lord of heaven, is asked to take away crown and throne, to lay on him a heavy guilt that will not leave his body, to end his reign in sighing and tears and to decree for him a life like death (xliii 41–63). Adad, lord of abundance, is asked to take away the rain and the flood-water, to destroy his land with famine and hunger, to storm against his city and to turn his land into a mound of the flood (xliii 64–80, which runs on into the next part). The stele is read through Harper’s 1904 transliteration and his plates; the readings of a number of verbs are his and uncertain, and the notes say which.

sentences.l: Ea, the-prince the-great, whose fates in-front go,
sentences.i: Ea, the great prince, whose decrees go in front,
sentences.n: A new god is called, and a new paragraph of curses begins. Ea is written {d}EN.KI, as in epilogue-1. rubûm “prince” is the single sign NUN (Harper’s glossary lists RUBÛ [NUN] at this very line); ra-bi-um is syllabic rabûm “great”. ša šīmātūšu is “whose fates”, šīmtum (plural šīmātum, as in mušīm šīmātim, xlii 53) + -šu. ina maḫra illakā is “in front they go”: illakā is the present of alākum, 3rd feminine plural, agreeing with šīmātūšu; maḫra is Harper’s maḫru “front, before”. The picture, a god whose decrees lead, is Harper’s sense and the exact force of ina maḫra is UNCERTAIN.

sentences.l: leader of-the-gods, who-knows everything its-name, who-lengthens
sentences.i: the leader of the gods, who knows everything there is, who lengthens
sentences.n: abkal ilī “leader of the gods”. abkal is the two signs NUN.ME (Harper’s glossary ABKALLU “wise one, leader” [NUN.ME], at this line; on the plate NUN is the hatched sign with its upright wedge, then ME), and ilī is the doubled sign NI.NI, as at xlii 22. mūdi mimma šumšu is the phrase of the litany, “who knows whatever its name”, that is, everything. mušarriku is the Š participle of arākum “to be long” (Harper’s arāku III,1), “who lengthens”; what he lengthens stands at the top of the next column (xliii 1), so this unit ends mid-sentence, as the column does. The final -u is a nominative vowel kept in the construct, as in mušarbû (xlii 57).

sentences.l: the-days-of my-life; understanding and wisdom let-him-turn-away-from-him-and,
sentences.i: the days of my life; may he turn understanding and wisdom away from him, and
sentences.n: ūm balṭīya “the days of my life” is the object of mušarriku at the end of the last column. ūm is written UD-um (Harper’s glossary ÛMU lists UD-um at this line), the construct form “day(s) of”; balṭīya is balāṭum “life” + -ia “my” (Harper’s balāṭu). Then a new wish, with the verb last: uznam u nēmeqam litēršuma. uznum is “ear”, and by extension “understanding” (the accusative, uz-na-am on the plate: UZ, NA, AM); nēmeqam is “wisdom” (nemēqum, as in epilogue-1; the GA sign is read qa₂). litēršuma is the precative of the D-stem of târum + -šu + -ma “and”, rendered as in epilogue-2 (“let him turn away from him”); that sense is UNCERTAIN, as there.

sentences.l: into-oblivion let-him-bring-him; his-rivers at-the-source let-him-dam-up,
sentences.i: and bring him to oblivion; may he dam up his rivers at the source,
sentences.n: ina mišītim littarrūšu: mišītim is Harper’s mišîtu “oblivion”, genitive after ina. littarrūšu is Harper’s târu I,2, li- + a t-stem form of târum “to turn, return” + -šu “him”; the form is UNCERTAIN (the ending -ru-šu looks plural, but the clause is read with one subject, the god, because the next clauses have one), and so is the exact sense “bring him to oblivion”. nārātīšu “his rivers” is the sign group A.ENGUR (ÍD, “river”) written twice, ÍD.ÍD-šu, a doubled sign marking the plural, as NI.NI does for ilī; nārum “river”, plural nārātum. ina nagbim is “at the source”: na-ak-bi-im is Harper’s nakbu “spring, source” (the AK sign; modern nagbum, as in the litany). liskir is the precative of sekērum (Harper’s sakâru) “to dam up”.

sentences.l: in his-land Ašnan, the-life of-the-people, may-not he-cause-to-be.
sentences.i: May he not let Ašnan, the life of the people, come into being in his land.
sentences.n: ina erṣetīšu “in his land” (erṣetum, here the plain word for land, + -šu). Ašnan is written {d}ŠE.TIR: the star is the divine determinative, ŠE is the chevron-stack sign and TIR the chevron-stack-with-hatch of Harper’s list no. 145; his glossary lists AN.ŠE.TIR, ašnan, at this line. Ašnan is the god of grain, which is why the next words call him “the life of the people”: napišti nišī (napištum “life”, nišū “people”). a u-ša-ab-ši is ay ušabši: ay “may not” with a preterite, as in epilogue-1, and ušabši the Š of bašûm “to be”, “let (him) bring into being”. So the curse is famine.

sentences.l: Šamaš, the-judge the-great of-heaven and-earth, who-guides those-set-with-life, lord of-trust,
sentences.i: Šamaš, the great judge of heaven and earth, who guides all living creatures, lord of trust,
sentences.n: The next god, Šamaš (the sign UTU). dajjānum rabûm is “the great judge” (syllabic, as Harper’s glossary lists it at this line); ša šamê u erṣetim “of heaven and earth”. muštēšir is the Št participle of ešērum “to be straight” (the same verb as šutēšurum in the litany), “who guides aright”, here written mu-uš-te-še-ir. šaknāt napištim is literally “those set (with) life”: šaknāt, from šakānum “to set, place”, feminine plural, + napištim “of life”; it is read as “living creatures”, which is Harper’s sense, UNCERTAIN in its grammar. bēlum tukulti is “lord of trust”: tukulti (tu-kul-ti, with the GUL sign read kul, Harper’s list no. 164) is Harper’s tukultu “strength”, modern “support, reliance”; “trust” is my choice.

sentences.l: his-kingship let-him-overthrow, his-case may-not he-judge, his-path let-him-confuse, the-foundation of-his-army let-him-destroy,
sentences.i: may he overthrow his kingship; may he not judge his case; may he lead his path astray; may he destroy the foundation of his army,
sentences.n: Four wishes, each ending in its verb. šarrūssu liskip: šarrūssu is šarrūtum + -šu (t + š said ss, written ZU, as in epilogue-2), liskip the precative of sakāpum “to overthrow” (Harper’s sakâpu). dīnšu ay idīn: dīnum “case” + -šu, ay “may not”, idīn the preterite of dânum “to judge”: “may he not judge his case”. urḫušu liši: urḫum “path” (Harper’s urḫu) + -šu; liši is Harper’s ešû “to confuse, cause to err”, UNCERTAIN in form and sense. išid ummānišu lišḫelṣi: išid is the sign SUḪUŠ “foundation” (Harper’s išid, as in the glossary at this line), ummānišu “his army”, and lišḫelṣi, Harper’s ḫalṣû III,1 “to destroy”, the Š precative of ḫalāṣum (UNCERTAIN; the sign ZI is read ṣi). The sign for el is partly drawn in dots on the plate (damaged on the stone), which is why Harper brackets [el].

sentences.l: in his-sight an-omen evil of-the-uprooting the-foundation-of his-kingship and of-the-loss of-his-land let-him-set for-him.
sentences.i: may he set before his eyes for him an evil omen of the uprooting of the foundation of his kingship and the loss of his land.
sentences.n: ina bīrišu is “in his sight” (Harper’s bīru “vision, view”, + -šu). šīram lemnam is “an evil omen” (Harper’s glossary ŠÎRU “oracle”, at this line): šīram is written with the sign UZU, Harper’s list no. 80, on the plate as the hatched sign and the diamond-and-arrow sign together (the identification with UZU is TENTATIVE), and lim-nam is lemnam “evil”. ša nasāḫ išid šarrūtišu u ḫalāq mātišu: ša + two infinitives in the construct, nasāḫ “uprooting” and ḫalāq “loss”, “(an omen) of the uprooting of the foundation of his kingship and the loss of his land”; išid is again SUḪUŠ. liškunšum is the G precative of šakānum + -šum “for him”, “let him set for him”. Line 30 has a second tier on the plate (Harper’s {b}) for li-iš-ku-un-šum.

sentences.l: a-word grievous of Šamaš quickly let-it-reach-him,
sentences.i: may the grievous word of Šamaš quickly overtake him,
sentences.n: awātum marūštum ša Šamaš is “the grievous word of Šamaš”, the curse; awātum is singular here (“word”), marūštum “grievous” (Harper’s glossary lists marūštu at this line, “blighting”). arḫiš is “quickly”. likšussu is the precative of kašādum “to reach, overtake” + -šu “him”, the d of the stem and the š of the suffix said ss and written ZU (li-ik-šu-zu).

sentences.l: above among-the-living let-him-uproot-him,
sentences.i: above, may he uproot him from among the living,
sentences.n: elîš is “above” (as in epilogue-1), ina baltūtim “among the living” (Harper’s baltu “living”). lissuḫšu is the precative of nasāḫum “to uproot”, with the n assimilated (as lissuḫ in epilogue-2) + -šu “him”; the sign ZU stands for ss and the whole is li-iz-zu-uḫ-šu, GISH read iz, ZU, AḪ read uḫ.

sentences.l: below in-the-earth his-spirits of-water let-him-deprive.
sentences.i: below, in the earth, may he deprive his spirits of water.
sentences.n: šaplîš “below”, ina erṣetim “in the earth”. ekimmêšu “his spirits (of the dead)” is the doubled sign GEKIM.GEKIM (Harper’s list no. 203; modern GIDIM, ekimmu; Harper’s glossary EKIMMU [GEKIM.GEKIM]-su at this line): the double sign marks the plural, and the sign identification is TENTATIVE. mê lišazmi is “let him deprive (them) of water”: lišazmi is the Š precative of zamûm “to lack, be deprived” (Harper’s zamû III,1), taking two accusatives; the dead in Mesopotamia depended on offerings of water poured by the living (background, not in the text).

sentences.l: Sîn, lord of-heaven, the-god my-creator, whose scimitar among-the-gods shines,
sentences.i: Sîn, lord of heaven, the god who created me, whose scimitar shines forth among the gods,
sentences.n: The third god, Sîn, written {d}EN.ZU, as in the litany. bēl šamê “lord of heaven”. ilum bānî is “the god, my creator”: DINGIR (the AN sign alone) for ilum, and bānî, the participle of banûm “to create” + -ī “my” (as bānîšu “his creator” in the litany). ša šērissu ina ilī šūpât: Harper’s glossary lists two nouns šērtu here, “sin” (xliii 48) and “sword, scimitar” (this line, 43), both spelled še-ri-zu; šērissu is šērtum + -šu, and “scimitar” (a weapon of the moon-god, or his crescent) is Harper’s sense and UNCERTAIN. ina ilī is “among the gods” (NI.NI again), and šūpât is the stative of the Š of wapûm (Harper’s “to shine”), “is made to appear, shines forth”.

sentences.l: the-crown, the-throne of kingship let-him-turn-away-from-him.
sentences.i: may he turn the crown and the throne of kingship away from him.
sentences.n: agâm kussâm ša šarrūtim: “the crown, the throne of kingship”, two accusatives side by side; litēršu as at xliii 4. UNCERTAIN, the signs: Harper normalises the two words as agâm and kussâm and prints no hyphens (the scan of his page is washed out here). I read agâm as the syllabic a-ga-am (the litany spells “crown” a-gi-im) and kussâm as {giš}GU.ZA as in laws-1-10, which is how Harper’s glossary treats kussû; on the plate the upper tier of this tall row has five sign-groups, which I could not match one for one with these six signs. The raised mark before ša, which in the washed-out scan looks like a footnote 1, is Harper’s raised b, and the plate shows what it means: line 45 is a tall row of two tiers, and ša šar-ru-tim stands on the lower.

sentences.l: a-guilt heavy, his-sin great, which in his-body not will-vanish, let-him-lay-on-him-and,
sentences.i: and lay on him a heavy guilt, a great sin of his, that will not leave his body,
sentences.n: Two accusatives: arnam kabtam “a heavy guilt” and šērissu rabītam “his great sin” (šērtum “sin”, Harper’s glossary at line 48; šērissu is šērtum + -šu). ša ina zumrišu lā iḫalliqu is “which will not vanish in his body” (zumrum “body”, iḫalliqu the present of ḫalāqum with the subjunctive -u; Harper prints the ending -ku, read qu₂). limussuma is Harper’s emēdu II,1 “to lay upon” (li-mu-zu-ma), li- + a form of emēdum + -šu + -ma “and”, “let him lay upon him”; Harper analyses it as a D-stem and the vowel u of the spelling is not explained, so the form is UNCERTAIN.

sentences.l: the-days the-months of-the-years of-his-reign in sighing and tears let-him-end, the-burden of-kingship let-him-increase for-him,
sentences.i: may he bring the days, months and years of his reign to an end in sighing and tears, and increase for him the burden of kingship,
sentences.n: ūmī arḫī is “days, months”: UD-mi, then the sign ITI twice. Harper prints arḫi arḫi, and the plate shows the doubled ITI, which is how the plural “months” is written (as NI.NI, ilī); so “arḫi arḫi” is one word, arḫī. šanāt palêšu is “the years of his reign” (palûm, BALA, + -šu). ina tanēḫim u dimmatim “in sighing and weeping” (as palê tanēḫim in epilogue-2; dimmatum “tears, lament”). lišaqti is the Š precative of qatûm “to come to an end” (Harper’s qatû III,1, “to bring to an end, cut off”; AK read aq), “let him bring to an end”. kammal šarrūtim is Harper’s kammalu “burden, ignominy” + “of kingship”, and lišaddilšu the D precative of šadālum “to extend, multiply” (Harper’s šadālu II,1) + -šu; “increase the burden” is my reading, UNCERTAIN.

sentences.l: a-life which with death is-equal into fate let-him-decree-for-him.
sentences.i: may he decree for him as his fate a life that is the equal of death.
sentences.n: balāṭam ša itti mūtim šitannu: “a life which … with death”. mūtim is mūtum “death” (not mutum “husband”, as in epilogue-2), and šitannu is Harper’s šanānu I,2 “to be like, to rival”, a t-stem used here as the relative clause’s verb: “which is the match of death”; UNCERTAIN in form. ana šīmtim lišīmšum is “let him decree for him as fate” (as in epilogue-2).

sentences.l: Adad, lord of-abundance, regent of-heaven and-earth, my-helper,
sentences.i: Adad, lord of abundance, regent of heaven and earth, my helper,
sentences.n: The fourth god, Adad, written {d}IM, as in laws-42-51. bēl ḫegallim “lord of abundance” (ḪÉ.GÁL-im, as in the litany). gugal šamê u erṣetim is “the regent (gugallum) of heaven and earth” (Harper’s glossary GUGALLU “regent”, syllabic gu-gal), the title of the god who oversees the canals. rēṣūa is rēṣum “helper” + -ūa “my” (the nominative before -ia; Harper’s ri-zu-u-a, ZU read ṣu).

sentences.l: rains in the-heaven, the-flood in the-source let-him-turn-away-from-him,
sentences.i: may he take away from him the rain of the sky and the flood-water of the springs,
sentences.n: zunnī ina šamê mīlam ina nagbim litēršu: the two water sources of the land, the rain of the sky and the flood (mīlum, Harper’s “water-flood”) of the springs (ina nagbim, as at xliii 8), are the objects of litēršu, “let him turn away from him”, as in epilogue-2, so the curse is drought; the Ea curse above dammed the rivers. zu-ni is Harper’s zunnu “rain”, plural form zunnī; reading these two phrases as parallel is mine and the grammar allows others. Rows 70 and 71 of the plate are the lines Harper prints as 70 and 71, so this unit has no division problem; the troubled lines follow.

sentences.l: his-land with-famine and hunger let-him-destroy,
sentences.i: may he destroy his land with famine and hunger,
sentences.n: mātassu ina ḫušaḫḫim u bubūtim liḫalliq: mātassu is mātum + -šu (ma-zu, ZU for ss, as at xlii 75); ḫušaḫḫim “famine” as in epilogue-2; bubūtim “hunger” (Harper’s bûbûtu); liḫalliq the D precative of ḫalāqum “to destroy”. PLATE (Harper’s provisional spot XLIII 70–74): Harper’s print has one divider too few, giving four pieces of text (ina nagbim | litēršu | ma-zu ina ḫušaḫḫim | u bubūtim | liḫalliq) for the five stele lines 70 to 74. This unit follows his printed division (72 ma-zu i-na ḫu-ša-aḫ-ḫi-im, 73 u bu-bu-tim, then 75 li-ḫal-li-iq). On Plates 79 and 80 the ruled rows are in fact five, 70 i-na na-ak-bi-im, 71 li-te-ir-šu, 72 ma-zu (two signs, one at each end of the row), 73 i-na ḫu-ša-aḫ-ḫi-im, 74 u bu-bu-tim, and then 75 li-ḫal-li-iq; so on the stone ma-zu stands alone on line 72 and i-na ḫu-ša-aḫ-ḫi-im on line 73. The line-break marks here keep Harper’s division only because the text file this part is checked against carries it.

sentences.l: against his-city furiously let-him-storm-and,
sentences.i: may he storm furiously against his city, and
sentences.n: eli ālišu “against his city” (the sign URU + -šu, as ḫalāq ali-šu in epilogue-2). izziš is “furiously”, the adverb in -iš from izzum “furious”. lissima is Harper’s nisû I,1 “to break loose, to storm” (li-is-si) + -ma “and”; the verb is UNCERTAIN, and “storm” suits the storm-god.

sentences.l: his-land into-a-mound of-the-flood let-him-turn.
sentences.i: may he turn his land into a mound of the flood.
sentences.n: The last unit of the part. mātassu ana tīl abūbim litēr: tīl abūbim “mound of the flood” (Harper’s telu “hill, heap”, written til with the BAD sign; abūbum “the flood”, the Deluge), the mound of ruins left by a flood; litēr is the D precative of târum “to turn”, here with ana, “let him turn into”. The sentence of curses of Adad goes on in the next part.
